⭐️ BlackRock wants tokenized funds to back traditional Wall Street trades 

📣 BlackRock has identified the use of tokenized investment funds as trading collateral in traditional financial markets as a potential next application for blockchain technology, building on existing arrangements that already allow institutional crypto traders to pledge tokenized fund holdings. Dan Maley, BlackRock’s head of cash management for Asia Pacific, said the firm’s tokenized funds are already being used as collateral in digital-asset markets. Extending that capability into conventional financial markets remains more complicated, although the asset manager sees opportunities for investors to transfer fund holdings without first redeeming them for cash.

🔔 The development moves BlackRock’s discussion beyond issuing digital representations of traditional investment products. Its focus now includes how those assets could function within the systems financial institutions use to settle transactions, secure trading positions and manage available cash. Collateral plays an established role in financial markets because banks, brokers and clearing firms require assets to secure loans, derivatives positions and other transactions. Investors commonly provide cash or eligible securities, with each receiving institution setting rules for the assets it will accept.

🔗 BlackRock sees a potential role for tokenized money market fund shares in that process. A tokenized share represents an interest in an investment fund while allowing certain transactions involving that interest to take place through blockchain infrastructure. In the Bloomberg interview, Maley described the opportunity to bring tokenized funds into the traditional financial ecosystem. He distinguished the collateral arrangements already operating in cryptocurrency markets from the more difficult work of connecting blockchain-based assets with established financial systems.

🔊 President Pezeshkian urges ambassadors to prioritize diplomacy, implementation of agreements

📌 Tehran, IRNA — President Masoud Pezeshkian has called on Iran’s newly appointed ambassadors to pursue diplomatic engagement, strengthen bilateral relations and ensure the implementation of agreements with their host countries.

President Pezeshkian made the remarks on Tuesday at a farewell ceremony for Iran’s incoming ambassadors to Kyrgyzstan, New Zealand, Japan, Burkina Faso and Cyprus, wishing them success in their diplomatic assignments.
​
He stressed that Iranian diplomatic missions should actively pursue constructive engagement despite obstacles, restrictions and attempts to undermine diplomatic efforts, making full use of available opportunities to expand bilateral relations and joint cooperation.
​
The president emphasized that ambassadors’ responsibilities should extend beyond political contacts to include identifying mutual capacities and facilitating the implementation of existing agreements and memorandums of understanding.
​
He said economic, trade, scientific and cultural cooperation, along with other areas of mutual interest, should feature prominently in their diplomatic agendas.
​
President Pezeshkian also called for the effective use of regional and international organizations to promote cooperation with host countries, highlighting the importance of engaging the private sector and business communities in expanding economic and commercial ties.
​
He said Iranian diplomatic missions should develop a thorough understanding of the economic, scientific and cultural potential of their host countries and facilitate effective connections between government institutions, businesses and private-sector actors on both sides.
​
During the ceremony, Iran’s ambassadors outlined cooperation opportunities in their respective countries and reaffirmed their commitment to implementing the government’s foreign policy and expanding bilateral relations.
​
The newly appointed envoys are Zahra Saei to Kyrgyzstan, Hamid Nirabadi to New Zealand, Mohammadreza Nazeri to Japan, Hossein Taghdar to Burkina Faso and Mohsen Shamsizadeh to Cyprus.

Crypto Idea

Gold is widely considered the ultimate safe-haven asset. But something interesting is happening right now. Despite high oil prices, geopolitical tensions, and a falling stock market, gold itself has dropped to a three-month low, losing around 4% in a single week.

The reason is pretty simple. High oil prices are fueling inflation again. The higher inflation goes, the more likely the Fed is to keep interest rates elevated or raise them further. And gold doesn't generate any interest income on its own. When bonds and the dollar start offering more attractive returns, some money flows in that direction instead.

There's a second factor, too. When markets sell off sharply, investors sometimes have to sell just about everything to cover losses and meet margin calls. That's why even gold can temporarily fall alongside stocks during periods of severe market stress. And that's exactly the kind of price action we're seeing right now.

And here's the key takeaway. A safe-haven asset isn't necessarily an asset that rises during every crisis. Gold performs well against some risks and less well against others. It can provide protection against currency problems, debt crises, and financial instability, while simultaneously coming under pressure from high interest rates and a strong dollar.

That's why it's worth rethinking gold as an all-purpose hedge. Before buying any safe-haven asset, it is important to first understand exactly which risk needs to be hedged. Because the very same crisis can make gold either the best-performing asset in portfolio or, at least temporarily, one of the worst.
